summary: Round 10, decomposition commit, no code and no tests. Re-reviewed only the two changes since my round-9 pass, both of which I verified against the tree rather than accepting. (1) The deletion of the round-8 half-clause is CORRECT and loses nothing my request was protecting. I measured all three of the production reviewer's grounds: ChainReplay.applyChain:369-383 LISTs with startAfter = keyFor(hop.from()-1) and GETs every entry key from the seeded checkpoint forward on every recovery, so harvesting pod state from the uncheckpointed tail costs zero additional requests -- the clause's 'COST gap' was false; M4.10b's third property (backlog-notes.md:222-228) is scoped to COMMIT-PATH requests, and the tail harvest happens in recovery, so that property never applied to it; and the tail cannot answer a (podId, flushSeq) replay at all, because nothing on the chain carries flushSeq -- CommitDelta(sequence, segments), SegmentCommit(segmentKey, runs), RunCommit(key, recordCount, firstOffset) -- making it an information gap by definition, exactly as the deletion says. The thing my round-8 request was actually protecting was the PROHIBITION on answering a replay by walking the chain backwards, and that prohibition survives verbatim at backlog-notes.md:226-227 inside M4.10b's cost property, which is the row that owns the mechanism decision and which M4.10d is hard-blocked on. Redundancy was lost; no constraint was. (2) The corrected fact in the rounds entry is true against the tree: crossFromCheckpoint seeds offsets from the checkpoint and the resulting Hop starts the LIST after the covered entries (the Hop javadoc at ChainReplay.java:48-52 says they 'are never GET at all'), so a replay older than the newest checkpoint has nothing left on the chain to read -- which is a sound justification for M4.10d's fold and a stronger one than the sentence it replaces. I also re-verified the test-facing tree claims the rows make, because they are what an implementer will build a failing test from, and all four hold: the Math::max fold in ChainReplay.fold:441 makes an offsets-only assertion structurally blind to a re-append at original absolute offsets; CommitLog.java:329-334 constructs, PUTs and returns one CommitDelta, so there is no append/return seam today; CheckpointWriterContentTest:141-157 is red today under the prescribed inversion ({podb=0} missing poda=42), so no K change is needed; and CheckpointWriterContentTest:116-129 replays strictly lower (9 then 4), so the '<' for '<=' mutant M4.10d names genuinely survives the existing fixture. Landable.

findings.title: M4.10d's surviving sentence enumerates exactly the ingredients of the chain walk M4.10b forbids, and no longer names the prohibition itself
findings.failure_scenario: The sentence now reads 'Only flushSeq is absent from the chain: SegmentKey puts podShortId and a per-pod sequence inside the segment key that every SegmentCommit carries, and each RunCommit carries the original offsets.' Read alone -- and backlog.md's M4.10d row links #m410d, and AGENTS.md tells a session to read the entry for the ONE task it picks -- that is a list of the two things a segment-key-keyed dedup would need: the key is on the chain and the original offsets are on the chain. An implementer can satisfy every assertion M4.10d prescribes by resolving a replay with a backwards scan for the segment key, which is precisely the fault M4.10b's cost property names in GETs. I am NOT asking for the deleted clause back -- it was false as written, and I verified that. The prohibition is intact at line 226-227, M4.10d is hard-blocked on M4.10b, and M4.10d's backlog row says the reach is 'bounded by what M4.10b makes durable', so the door is closed by ordering. This is a redundancy I would have kept, not a gap: if it were restated, the true form is that the walk is USELESS for flushSeq, not merely expensive. Non-blocking, and belongs in M4.10d's commit rather than in another round here.
findings.suggestion: Optional, at M4.10d pickup: end the sentence with a pointer such as 'and M4.10b's cost property forbids resolving a replay by scanning for either'.

findings.title: the tripwire's method NAME becomes false when M4.10d inverts the assertion, and the gate that exists to catch this cannot see it either way -- confirmed, still M4.10d's
findings.failure_scenario: Measured against scripts/test_integrity.py's STRENGTH table: doesNotContainKey appears in no pattern and scores 0, containsEntry scores 2. So (a) the prescribed inversion registers as a STRENGTHENING and check-test-integrity.sh will not fire on M4.10d, and (b) the failure the row warns about -- DELETING the tripwire instead of inverting it -- leaves theFirstCheckpointAfterATakeoverCarriesNoPodsAtAll:141-157 with its other assertion (containsEntry('poda', 42L), strength 2) intact, so the method's score is UNCHANGED and the gate reports 'no test weakened'. The rule is therefore carried by this row's prose and by nothing else, which is the correct place for it and confirms the row is doing work no gate can. What remains unsaid is that the method NAME and CheckpointWriter's class javadoc (CheckpointWriter.java:49-55, which names CheckpointWriterContentTest as the tripwire) both become false statements the moment the assertion inverts, and a stale name over an inverted assertion is how the next reader mis-reads the fixture. Belongs to M4.10d, the commit that inverts it; my round-9 judgement stands.
findings.suggestion: At M4.10d: rename the method and update CheckpointWriter's class javadoc in the same commit as the inversion.

findings.title: M4.10d's row never names FakeSequencer, and the fake's standing obligation is pinned to an ID that is now a 'split' row with no implementer
findings.failure_scenario: FakeSequencer's class javadoc says idempotency on (podId, flushSeq) 'is M4.10's task and lands here in the same commit as the real behaviour so the two cannot drift', and Sequencer's contract says 'it does not yet'. After this commit M4.10 is a split banner nobody implements; the commit that changes the behaviour is M4.10d, whose row and notes mention neither file. If M4.10b answers 'no format change' then M4.10c is void and non-negotiable 8 -- the rule that would otherwise drag the fakes along -- never fires, so nothing in the tree forces the fake to be updated. The concrete failure: LocalSequencer refuses a replay, FakeSequencer assigns it fresh offsets, and every downstream test written against the testFixtures double passes while the real sequencer behaves differently -- the divergence the fake's own javadoc calls 'worse than no fake at all'. Non-blocking for a decomposition commit; the obligation is recorded in the tree, just under the wrong ID.
findings.suggestion: One clause in M4.10d's notes: the fake and Sequencer's 'it does not yet' note land in the same commit as the refusal.
